title: Prothalamion: title and occasion
greek: Gk pro + thalamos, before the bridal chamber
short: A 'spousal verse' for the double betrothal of Lady Elizabeth and Lady Katherine Somerset, married at Essex House on 8 November 1596.
body: 'Prothalamion' appears to be Spenser's coinage, formed on the model of 'epithalamion' (song at the bridal chamber) with Greek pro, 'before'; it is a song preceding the wedding. The full title calls it a 'Spousall Verse' in honour of the double marriage of Lady Elizabeth and Lady Katherine Somerset, daughters of Edward Somerset, 4th Earl of Worcester, to Henry Guildford and William Petre. The weddings took place at Essex House on 8 November 1596; the poem, printed by William Ponsonby in 1596, imagines the brides' journey down the Thames to the house of the Earl of Essex, its probable patron.

title: Zephyrus ... Titans beames
short: The gentle west wind (Zephyrus) cools the sun's heat; 'Titan' is a classical name for the sun-god.
body: Zephyrus is the west wind, bringer of spring in classical poetry. 'Titan' is an epithet of the sun (Sol or Helios, son of the Titan Hyperion) used by Ovid and Virgil. The wind 'delays' (tempers, allays) the heat. The opening thus sets an idealised summer day, although the actual wedding was in November; critics note that the poem's season is symbolic, matching the later pun on 'Somers-heat'. 'Glyster' means glitter or shine.

title: sullein care ... long fruitlesse stay in Princes Court
short: The poet's disappointment at court, where he had waited in vain for preferment during his visit to London in 1596.
body: Spenser came to England from Ireland in 1595-6, partly to see the second instalment of The Faerie Queene through the press. These lines express bitterness at his 'long fruitlesse stay' at court and 'expectation vayne' of reward, a complaint he also makes in Colin Clouts Come Home Againe and Mother Hubberds Tale. Critics have often noted that this personal grievance, unusual in a marriage poem, gives Prothalamion its elegiac undertone. 'Sullein' means gloomy, sullen; the image of hopes flying 'like empty shaddowes' recalls classical descriptions of the shades of the dead.

title: Sweete Themmes! runne softly
short: The refrain closing each of the ten stanzas, later quoted by T. S. Eliot in The Waste Land.
body: Each of the ten eighteen-line stanzas ends with a refrain addressing the Thames, preceded by a line about the bridal day 'which is not long' (that is, not far off). The tense and wording shift slightly ('was not long', 'should not be long'), and editors have noted the ambiguity of 'not long', which can also suggest the brevity of joy. The river is personified as a gentle male deity whose flow accompanies and measures the song. T. S. Eliot quotes the line in 'The Fire Sermon' of The Waste Land (1922, l. 176), setting Spenser's idealised river against the litter of the modern Thames.

title: rutty
short: Probably 'rooty', full of roots; some editors gloss it as rutted or furrowed.
body: Editors usually gloss 'rutty' as 'rooty', covered with tree and plant roots, which suits a river bank; the OED records a separate sense of rutted. The bank 'hemmes' (borders) the river and is 'paynted' with 'variable' (varied, many-coloured) flowers. The 'daintie gemmes' of the meadows are flowers, compared to jewels fit to adorn maidens' bowers and to crown their 'Paramours' (lovers, a word without the later suggestion of illicit love).

title: A Flocke of Nymphes ... Daughters of the Flood
short: River nymphs (naiads), daughters of the Thames, with loose green-tinged hair like brides.
body: The nymphs are naiads, daughters of the river god, a classical motif Spenser had used at length in the marriage of Thames and Medway (The Faerie Queene IV.xi). Their 'greenish locks' are the colour of river weed; loose, untied hair was the sign of a bride in English custom, hence 'As each had bene a Bryde'. The scene of maidens gathering flowers in a meadow has classical antecedents in Proserpina's flower-gathering (Ovid, Metamorphoses 5) and in the pastoral tradition.

title: entraylèd curiously ... flasket ... feateously
short: Intricately interlaced wicker baskets ('flaskets'); the nymphs pick flowers 'feateously', deftly.
body: 'Entrailed' means interlaced or entwined, from Old French entreillier (to trellis), and 'curiously' means with careful, intricate art. A 'flasket' is a long shallow basket. 'Feateously' means deftly, neatly (from 'feat', skilful). Spenser's archaic diction, much criticised by Ben Jonson for 'writing no language', is deliberate here: it gives the scene the texture of old English pastoral, the manner of The Shepheardes Calender.

title: Violet ... Dazie ... Lillie ... vermeil Roses
short: A catalogue of symbolic flowers: violet, daisy that closes at evening, virgin lily, true primrose, and bright red ('vermeil') roses.
body: 'Vermeil' is vermilion, bright red. The flowers carry conventional associations: the lily of virginity, the primrose 'trew' (perhaps of fidelity), the rose of love, and the daisy, 'day's eye', which closes at evening. Spenser had produced a famous flower catalogue in the April eclogue of The Shepheardes Calender. The flowers are gathered for the 'Bridegromes posies', bunches or nosegays, and later strewn on the swans' path like a bride's chamber floor.

title: two Swannes
short: The two brides appear as white swans floating down the river, an emblem of purity, beauty and the Thames's own royal birds.
body: The brides are figured as two swans. The Thames swan was a familiar sight and protected by royal right; swans were emblems of purity, of Venus (whose chariot they draw) and of poets, since they were thought to sing before death. The allegory allows Spenser to stage a river pageant like the water processions of Elizabethan London without describing the actual brides, who probably made no such journey. The stanza's hyperboles of whiteness, outdoing the snows of Pindus and Jove's swan-disguise, prepare for the pun on their family name in stanza 4.

title: Pindus
short: The mountain range of northern Greece between Thessaly and Epirus, here a byword for snowy whiteness.
body: Pindus is the great mountain range of northern Greece, separating Thessaly from Epirus, and was associated with the Muses and Apollo. Its snow-capped summits provide a classical standard of whiteness which the swans surpass. The comparison typifies the poem's hyperbolic structure, in which each image is introduced only to be outdone ('Yet not so white as these, nor nothing neare').

title: Jove ... Leda
short: Jove took the shape of a swan to seduce Leda, mother of Helen and of the twins Castor and Pollux.
body: Jupiter took the form of a swan to approach Leda, wife of Tyndareus; from their union came Helen and the twins Castor and Pollux (Ovid, Metamorphoses 6.109). The swans of the poem are whiter even than Jove in disguise. The myth is erotic and even violent, and some critics see a sly hint of sexuality beneath the poem's purity; others stress that the allusion prepares for the closing comparison of the bridegrooms to 'the twins of Jove', Leda's sons.

title: Venus silver Teeme
short: Swans were said to draw the chariot of Venus through the sky.
body: In Ovid's account Venus drives a chariot drawn by swans (Metamorphoses 10.708 and 717-18, where she yokes her swans to fly to Cyprus). The nymphs think the birds are 'heavenly borne', or the very pair that draws the goddess of love, and even 'Angels'. The rapid climb from classical to Christian superlative is typical of Spenser's syncretism. The stanza then corrects itself: they were in fact 'bred of Somers-heat'.

title: Somers-heat
short: A pun on the brides' family name, Somerset: the swans were 'bred of summer's heat'.
body: The compound 'Somers-heat' puns on Somerset, the surname of the Earls of Worcester. The pun explains the otherwise strange summer setting of a November wedding: the swans are born of summer's heat because they are daughters of the house of Somerset. Such name-play was a standard compliment in Elizabethan occasional verse, and Spenser repeats it with Essex's name later in the poem.

title: Peneus ... Tempe ... Thessaly
short: The Peneus, river of the beautiful vale of Tempe in Thessaly, strewn with flowers like a bride's chamber floor.
body: The Peneus flows through the vale of Tempe in Thessaly, celebrated in ancient literature for its beauty; in Ovid the river god Peneus is the father of Daphne. The Thames, strewn with flowers, is compared to this classical landscape, and then, more domestically, to 'a Brydes Chamber flore', alluding to the English custom of strewing the bridal chamber with flowers and rushes. Spenser also places Tempe in the Epithalamion (Maia lying in Tempe).

title: couplement ... heart-quelling Sonne ... assoile
short: 'Couplement' is union, coupling; Cupid, Venus's 'heart-quelling Sonne', is asked to 'assoile' (absolve, remove) love's discords.
body: The nymph's song is a miniature epithalamium. 'Couplement' (union in pairs) is a rare word; Cupid is 'heart-quelling' because he subdues hearts; his smile has 'vertue' (power) to remove dislike and 'faultie guile', and to 'assoile' them, a word meaning to absolve or to dispel. The blessings asked, peace, plenty and fruitful issue that will 'confound' the families' foes, are the standard aims of the marriage hymn and echo the prayers of the Epithalamion.

title: undersong
short: A refrain or burden sung by the chorus in answer to the solo singer.
body: An 'undersong' is the burden or refrain of a song, sung beneath or after the main voice. The other nymphs 'redoubled' the singer's refrain, and Echo resounds it from the 'neighbour ground', recalling the echoing refrain of the Epithalamion. The river Lee, unable to speak, shows its 'glad affection' by slowing its stream, a fine instance of the poem's courteous personification of landscape.

title: the Lee
short: Either the river Lea, a tributary of the Thames, or simply 'the river' (the Thames) itself; editors disagree.
body: The Lea joins the Thames at Bow, east of the City, so a journey 'downe along the Lee' to the Temple would be geographically awkward. Some editors therefore take 'Lee' as a general word for a river or stream (or a meadow, 'lea') and refer it to the Thames; others accept a loose allusion to the Lea, which Spenser includes among the rivers of the Thames-Medway marriage canto (The Faerie Queene IV.xi). The personified Lee that 'murmurde low' and 'lackt a tong' (ll. 114-16, where the swans pass 'Adowne the Lee') is in either case the water on which the swans travel.

title: as Cynthia doth shend / The lesser starres
short: The two swans outshine the other birds as the moon puts the lesser stars to shame; 'shend' means disgrace or eclipse.
body: 'Shend' means to put to shame, disgrace, or (as here) to outshine. Cynthia is the moon and, in Elizabethan poetry, often a name for Queen Elizabeth herself (Ralegh's 'Cynthia', Spenser's own Colin Clouts Come Home Againe). The simile of the moon among the stars is classical (Horace, Odes 1.12.46-8, of the Julian star 'velut inter ignis luna minores'). 'Enrangèd' means set in ranks, arranged in order.

title: mery London, my most kyndly Nurse
short: Spenser was born in London, his 'natural' nurse; his name, he claims, came from 'another place', the noble Spencers of Althorp.
body: Spenser was born in London about 1552 and educated at Merchant Taylors' School. 'Kyndly' means natural, by birth (from 'kind', nature) as well as affectionate. 'Though from another place I take my name, / An house of auncient fame' is his claim of kinship with the Spencers of Althorp in Northamptonshire, whose daughters he praised in Colin Clouts Come Home Againe and to whom he dedicated several poems. The genealogical link is not documented, but the Spencers apparently accepted the compliment.

title: bricky towres ... the Templer Knights
short: The Temple, once house of the Knights Templar, by Spenser's day the Inns of Court where lawyers lived and studied.
body: The Temple, between Fleet Street and the Thames, was the London headquarters of the Knights Templar until the order was suppressed in 1312, partly on charges of corruption and pride ('Till they decayd through pride'). It later passed to the lawyers of the Inner and Middle Temple, two of the Inns of Court, the 'studious Lawyers' and their 'bowers' (chambers). 'Whylome' means formerly. The moral aside on the Templars' fall is one of several shadows the poem casts across its celebration.

title: a stately place ... that great Lord
short: Leicester House on the Strand, home of Spenser's former patron Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester (d. 1588), later Essex House.
body: Next to the Temple stood Leicester House, the London residence of Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, Queen Elizabeth's favourite, in whose household Spenser served around 1579-80 and from whom he 'gaynèd giftes and goodly grace'. After Leicester's death in 1588 the house passed to his stepson Robert Devereux, Earl of Essex, and was renamed Essex House; the Somerset weddings took place there. Spenser's lament for his 'freendles case' after Leicester's death is cut short: 'here fits not well / Olde woes, but joyes, to tell'.

title: a noble Peer ... Hercules two pillors
short: Robert Devereux, 2nd Earl of Essex, fresh from his capture of Cadiz in June 1596, whose fame shook Spain and the Straits of Gibraltar.
body: The 'noble Peer' is the Earl of Essex, who in June 1596 led, with Lord Howard of Effingham, the expedition that sacked Cadiz. 'Hercules two pillors' are the promontories at the Straits of Gibraltar (Calpe and Abyla), which Hercules was said to have set up at the edge of the known world; Cadiz lies just beyond them. Spenser praises Essex as 'flower of Chevalrie' and prays for his further victories, a political compliment that later readers find poignant, since Essex rebelled and was executed in 1601. Some critics see the passage as Spenser's bid for a new patron.

title: happinesse of thine owne name
short: A pun on Essex's family name, Devereux, heard as French 'heureux' (happy).
body: The phrase 'endlesse happinesse of thine owne name / That promiseth the same' is generally taken to pun on Devereux, the Earl's surname, as if from French 'heureux', happy (or 'devenir heureux'). As with 'Somers-heat', the compliment works by finding a prophecy in a name. The prayer that 'great Elisaes glorious name may ring / Through al the world' places Essex's glory under the Queen's, a necessary courtesy given Elizabeth's suspicion of her favourite's popularity.

title: Radiant Hesper
short: Essex emerges like the evening star after bathing in the ocean, a classical image of the star rising refreshed from the sea.
body: Hesper (Hesperus) is the evening star, the planet Venus. Classical poets imagined the stars bathing in Ocean before rising (Virgil, Aeneid 8.589-91, of Lucifer the morning star wet with Ocean's wave). The image presents Essex as glorious and as leading a train, as the evening star leads the other stars. Since Hesperus was traditionally invoked at weddings (as in Catullus 62, 'Vesper adest'), the comparison is also apt to the marriage theme.

title: the twins of Jove ... the Bauldricke of the Heavens
short: The bridegrooms are like Castor and Pollux, Jove's twin sons by Leda, set among the stars as Gemini in the zodiac (the heavens' 'baldric').
body: Castor and Pollux, the Dioscuri, were sons of Leda (Pollux by Jove), and after death became the constellation Gemini. A baldric is a belt worn diagonally across the body, and the 'Bauldricke of the Heavens' is the zodiac, the band of constellations crossing the sky, in which Gemini is one sign. The comparison neatly closes the swan imagery: the brides were whiter than Jove's swan, and the grooms are the swan's twin sons. The poem ends with the grooms, Henry Guildford and William Petre, receiving their brides 'at th' appointed tyde'.
